title: (Co)video killed the radio star
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Shaun Brien argues that the pandemic has become a catch-all excuse for everything wrong in schools, and that using it that way lowers the bar for students. He concedes real harms from remote learning and a few genuine gains, namely stronger pastoral and mental health support and better shared digital curriculum resources. His main complaint is that schools never rolled back device use after lockdowns and instead chased a digital hangover with more technology platforms. He sees lowered expectations in take-home assessments, no-homework policies, open-ended research tasks and shelved performance development, and sees teams drifting into separate islands. He also says the wellbeing pendulum has swung so far that opt-out opportunities widen the gap for the students who most need high expectations.
points: Blaming the lingering pandemic for current outcomes creates a soft bigotry of low expectations and replaces the interventions and planning that would actually repair the gaps.
Two real positives are the embedding of proactive wellbeing and funded counselling support, and high-quality shared digital curriculum banks that reduce workload for new teachers.
Schools never reversed the pandemic's device dependence and instead kept adding tech platforms, a sunk cost fallacy defended by the claim that students learn better on laptops.
Lowered expectations show up in take-home assessments, no-homework policies, open-ended research tasks and shelved performance development, which hits students most in need hardest.
Wellbeing practice has overshot in places, offering opt-outs in the name of trauma-informed care instead of high expectations paired with support.
quotes: However, explaining all student outcomes away using the pandemic effectively lowers the bar for students

Rather than put in interventions or strengthen our planning to fill the potholes which were created by the pandemic, we instead drive over them and hope for the first it doesn’t hurt our wheel alignment.

Schools have also been provided with funding to provide far more mental health support through both counsellors and psychologists which can help give student access to intervention which they may not be able to or feel comfortable with opting into outside of school.

Instead we’re left with somewhat of a digital hangover from the pandemic and we’ve been chasing it with the hair of the dog that bit us ever since. Results falling? There’s a tech platform to help with that!
Instead of increasing the pace and lifting expectations these students have instead been given take home assessments, no homework policies and class after class of open ended research tasks.
Instead of a team sport, it began to feel more like an individual event where you clock in and clock out without a second thought to the people around them.

it seems the pendulum has swung so far that instead of setting high expectations and creating opportunities for success for these students we just give them opportunities to opt out and make the gap get bigger.
